misconceptions.description: Believing novices learn best from unguided problem solving and that worked examples are a shortcut that weakens learning.
misconceptions.trigger: learner gives novices many open problems and no worked examples
misconceptions.feedback: For novices, the worked-example effect favors studying worked solutions first. Front-load worked examples, then fade toward open problems.

misconceptions.description: Treating fading as simply deleting worked examples rather than gradually transferring steps to the learner through completion problems.
misconceptions.trigger: learner jumps from full worked example straight to open problems with no completion step
misconceptions.feedback: Fading is gradual: insert completion problems that hand off some steps before full independence. It is a transfer of responsibility, not a sudden removal.

misconceptions.description: Assuming worked examples remain optimal for all learners at all times, ignoring the expertise-reversal effect.
misconceptions.trigger: learner keeps full worked support for advanced learners who already have schemas
misconceptions.feedback: Expertise reversal: continued full worked support becomes redundant for experienced learners. Fade support as prior knowledge grows.

misconceptions.description: Confusing a final-answer key with a worked example, omitting the intermediate steps and rationale that carry the learning value.
misconceptions.trigger: learner presents only the final answer and calls it a worked example
misconceptions.feedback: A worked example must show and explain the intermediate steps. An answer alone gives no schema to study.
